For the relatively little money paid - this is an OK receiver. My previous Sony of the similar basic level has been playing nicely the last 7 years, until it died, so I thought I'll follow-up with the brand. Well, there has been one disappointment, but big enough (for me, personally) to return it and try something different. Issue may be subjective, nevertheless... the issue is a quite flat sound, in particular the bass. The non-audiophile (i.e. reasonably priced) receivers used to have a "contour", or "bass boost" function (even the previous Sony model had it), which greatly enhanced the audibility of lower frequencies when played at low decibels. This one lacks it (and it sounds like most of nowadays sold receivers are like this), hence the sound coming out is quite flat (also for treble band), unless you go really loud. In addition, the receiver lacks a sub-woofer output, so there is no chance to improve low frequencies.
Out of the other available receivers, I decided to pick (by recommendation) a little more up-scale (yet still reasonably priced) Harman Kardon HK 3390 (2 x 80W) Stereo Receiver, which has sub-woofer outputs - even though it also lacks bass boost, I am expecting it will revive the bass, even with my old Sony 10" sub.

Indoors: Each unit sounds very different depending on where it is located. For the Emberton, it sounded a little too bassy in most locations and the mids and highs sounded drowned out because of that. The Bose also sounded a little too bassy but was more even on the mids and highs. In particular, the highs sounded great indoors. In certain spaces indoors, the Bose might have had the most even sound but only when standing right in front of the speaker. The JBL Flip 4 did not go as low in frequency response to the others however there was more clarity in the mids and had a more stereophonic sound. The Flip 4 in most cases sounded too bassy indoors (and I don't mean low bass but mid-bass). The Emberton sounded as one of the best when placed in the middle of the room. Outdoors: The Emberton was definitely the loudest and had the most bass and sounded better outdoors and had the best low frequency response as well as loudness. In some cases again, the bass drowned out the mids and highs. I liked the JBL Flip 4 outdoors for having a stereophonic sound and clarity in the mids and highs however the bass did not extend as low as the other 2. The Bose did not sound too good outdoors (worst of the 3 outdoors) and sounded the best indoors in particular situations. The Bose outdoors also did not perform well when not standing right in front of the speakers while the other 2, you can get pretty good response at different angles. As far as loudness and bass, the Emberton blew the other 2 away, but did not have the stereo spaciousness or mid/high clarity of the JBL.

I don't know exactly where this would fit into a birders toolkit. For me, I am planning on taking it to the tropics with the kids as a cheap and easy to carry spotting scope. I'm hoping that I can remove the camera and set this up on the tripod with a quick release plate and put it on non moving birds and sloths etcetera so they don't get too frustrated with their bins. And I don't break my back with both camera and full spotting scope.

I will say this, in the 90's I paid $49 for a Russian surplus spotting scope that did have 20x zoom, but in every other way it was far, far inferior to this monocular. This has the passable optics for a beginning birder still not looking to invest well. It is fairly sharp in the center of the image but less so at the edges. It has a very small depth of field, but a surprising close focus of 6-8 feet. I would not recommend this as a replacement for a full set of bins, but you are getting half a budget pair binoculars.

The focus is easy enough to adjust one handed and it seems fairly well constructed in the hand. I would not want to drop it and fully test it, but it seems sturdy enough. Lense covers are also fine. The eye cup raises and lowers for eyeglass wearers but the mechanism seems less quality than other aspects of the monocular. I question the focal length placement for the cup at full or minimum extension. It seems like the missed the proper marks.

I think it will work for what I was hoping for, a rainforest spotting aid and a reserve optics for the car, but not sure I would recommend for much else.

I've had several Amazon Basics' items since the line was introduced. Most have been quite good. Unfortunately this tripod wasn't one of them.

The feel is cheap and plastic-y. I wasn't expecting bearings in the pan-head but the plastic on plastic mechanisms are terrible.

I tested this item with my Kodak Z990 digital camera. It weighs approx. 21 oz. with batteries.

The camera mount has a good rubber pad for your camera to sit on and the tightening screw has a butterfly head so no screwdriver or coins are needed to attach/detach the mount from the camera. The mount attaches to the tripod with a spring-loaded release arm. There is actually very little contact area on the tripod itself (only two corners) holding the mount in place, also the release arm does NOT have a safety catch.

Pan Functionality - Fully tightened down I can still, with not much effort, swing the head from left to right. Fully loosened the motion is heavy and awkward easily upsetting the tripod's position. Tightening this knob fully actually interferes with the...

Tilt Functionality - The action is not much better here. You can lock the tilt angle into place and it does stay there. There's just as much plastic on plastic drag when in motion. The arm is generously long and comfortable to grip. The side-tilt mechanism goes reasonably easily from flat to 90°. It does not lock in place well.

Leg Functionality - The legs extend and retract with mild effort. They lock into place firmly. With just the larger leg section extended the tripod is fairly sturdy. Extending the smaller leg sections dramatically increases wobble. There is a weight/gear hook for added stabilization but it is plastic and feels easily broken. The swiveling rubber feet are innovative but only held on by friction and can easily become detached. The center stabilizer locks and unlocks easily with only a quarter turn and holds in place well. There is a serviceable carry handle attached to the leg mount section.

The tripod has two bubble levels. The first, a small button level is at the top of one of the leg mounts. The second, a tube level, is just under and inch long and is under and partially obscured by the camera mount. With a camera attached it becomes useless.

The center section extends and lowers via a crank mechanisms and locks in place with a plastic collar. There is no positive safety lock. Loosen the collar and your camera comes down rapidly on its own. Extending your camera this way will only increase the instability of this tripod.

The included carry bag reflects the quality of it's tripod. Its material is unpadded and thin. It has no extra pockets and the half-inch nylon shoulder strap is also unpadded making it rather uncomfortable to carry.

In conclusion... I wouldn't recommend this tripod even as a starter for someone just getting into photography it will only add frustration to the experience. Spend a little more and get a far better tripod or spend a little less and get something of equal quality.

I was really skeptical about getting one of the newer kindles since I was a die hard kindle fan when they first came out. I always like my electronics to have buttons and especially my kindle since I tend to read with one thumb on the screen itself I worried that if I upgraded to this, my thumb would either end up turning pages too soon or it wouldn't be sensitive enough to read my thumb when I wanted to. My old kindle no longer took a charge after 6 years so I had to upgrade and literally the only reason I went with this over anything else (I was wanting to get another one of my old kindles) was the backlight. I have insomnia so I'm often awake in bed with my snoring boyfriend next to me so having a light on isn't an option so having a kindle with a backlight would be ideal.

Turns out my worry over not having a button was all in vain! The touch screen has just the right amount of sensitivity. It's not so sensitive that resting my thumb on the screen where it's comfortable activates anything, but it's not so dull that I can't turn the pages easily. The back lighting is adjustable so I don't have to blind myself and I don't have to use it if I don't want to if I've got plenty of natural light. The screen is clear and crisp, it fits comfortably in my hand and the amount of books I can fit on there is insane! I've currently got 200 titles and I've still got plenty of room for more. It moves faster than my old kindle and the charge is amazing. I've been using it for over a month now and I'm still at 25% battery without charging it once aside from the day I received it.

This is by far the best kindle I've ever had!

This is a review of the product by the person I got it for:

Definitely is the actual size as shown on the box. Nice, compact size with a requirement of only one USB port. Installation was easy to follow and complete (follow the folder-finding path on the manual though, and don't just start clicking files when the hard-drive shows up under "My Computer"). For not being a particularly tech-savvy person myself, it was fairly easy to transfer files from my old hard-drive to the new one. Fast access; doesn't slow down my computer like my older one did. Completely satisfied with the product; very user friendly.

After reading the comments here, I decided to not bother with the Sony software. I installed "Nexus Media Importer" from the Google Android app store and it automatically detects and mounts the Sony device. I can read and write files with no problem, including playing audio and video files without copying them to the phone memory. On my PC, the Sony device mounts like any other flash drive. I would give this 5 stars if it was $30 (and if it came with better instructions), but the $45 price seems high for what is essentially a flash drive with a micro-USB port. You can get the same functionality (in a larger form factor) by using a regular flash drive and an OTG cable (sold here on Amazon for less than $2).

EDIT: I'm still happy with this device, but since writing this review, I've noticed that several other companies (SanDisk and others) have come out with similar products (flash drives with both micro and regular USB connectors) and some of them have much faster USB3.0 speeds. Sony has reduced their price to be competitive. Shop around; I expect functionality is similar.

I ordered the 'Nomodo U Wireless Wearable Bluetooth Speaker, Rechargeable and Portable' for review and would like to share some of my thoughts and experiences.
First off, out of the box this Bluetooth Wireless Speaker not only looks interesting but it is beautiful. I say interesting because I have never had a Wireless Speaker like this, and I wonder where would I use it and would it be practical. Well after some time with this device I must first report that it really does sound amazing. The sound is clean and immersive. It is hard to describe the incredible sound sensation while wearing it. It is almost as if you have speakers floating on either side of your head (pointing directly to your ears) and it is nothing like I have experienced before but it is pretty cool. I have been trying to think of how this Speaker would actually fit into my life. It's not like you are wearing headphones that only you can hear. While wearing this speaker, everyone else around you can hear it too but it's just not as immersive as it is to you. It's hard to describe, but what I will say is that it really is an incredible experience. If the volume is down low you can still hear your surroundings yet when you crank it up, surprisingly your surrounding sounds seem to disappear. Personally I have decided that this would be best worn while alone in your home while doing simple household chores. Like doing dishes or folding laundry. The Nomodo U speaker stays put pretty well for the most part due to the rubber neck pad, yet if you are constantly bending over or doing anything where you are moving around a lot and twisting your head and body, it tends to need re adjusted. Sitting in bed listening to Music or listening to an audio book works really well with this device as long as you wont be disturbing your partner. As for watching movies, for me this really doesn't work. I can't find anywhere where it says what version of Bluetooth this is using but I don't think it is Bluetooth 5.0 unfortunately. There are noticeable sync issues and this just gets annoying. Speaking of the Bluetooth, it connects/pairs effortlessly to all of my devices and that is a bonus. I am disappointed however that it uses Micro USB (the cable is included btw) for charging. With this being a new device it should have USB Type C. I always have to mention this with any new devices. Call quality is acceptable. Those on the other end can hear you just fine, as long as you are not in a loud environment. This is pretty typical with most wireless headphones. Overall I do love this device and think it is a great value for what it is.

I have worked with a number of trackballs, my most successful being a Logitech M570 which served me well for years. I finally wore it out and after some research I purchased the Logitech MX Ergo to replace it. I have had it about three days, and it has already proven to be exactly what I had hoped and more. It’s not perfect but it’s close.

I was attracted to the fact that it works both as a wireless mouse with a USB receiver as well as a Bluetooth mouse. I have two computers on my desk, one being a Windows 10 system and the other being a Linux (Arch-based) system. My old trackball worked with both though I had to move the receiver between the systems, so I went with the assumption that this one would also work with both.

I connected the trackball to my Windows system via Bluetooth and it has been flawless in operation. It connects without intervention and it works exactly as expected - all buttons work as they should and the operation is very smooth and predictable.

I plugged the USB receiver into the Linux machine, pushed the channel button on the trackball and it immediately started working on the Linux machine, even though it was still paired to the Windows system via Bluetooth. It works exactly as it should and I have had absolutely no issues with the trackball on my Linux installation. So now, I can switch back and forth between the two systems with the push of the channel button and without having to connect or disconnect anything. It simply works, and the switch-over is fast. The take-away for me is that I no longer need two mice on the desk.

I friend came over with his MacBook and there was no issue at all with connecting the trackball via USB. We did not try connecting via Bluetooth.

The trackball has a metal plate on the bottom that is held in place with magnets, and depending on how the plate is attached the trackball can be tilted to ease wrist strain. The plate serves another purpose too - it adds a lot of weight to the trackball. Even without the plate, the trackball is hefty and has some mass to it, but the plate just makes it even more so. For me that’s a positive; others may dislike the added weight.

One of the things I have missed has been a tilting scroll wheel. This trackball has one and I have been enjoying getting used to that feature again.

One thing I did notice is that there is no CD/DVD in the package for loading drivers. This isn’t a big deal, and it’s easy enough to get the drivers from the net. That said, the trackball just seems to work when you attach it, without any issue. For me it has absolutely been plug-and-play, on every system I have tried.

If I could change one thing - I would have made this trackball a little bigger. I have big hands and I struggle to find a trackball that’s an absolute perfect fit. This one is close. For the large majority of people it’s going to be spot on.

I am very happy with this trackball and have no issue with recommending it. It works great, connects easily, when connected to two different systems it switches at the press of a button, it has a bit of heft to it and the tilt is adjustable for wrist comfort. It’s really all I could ask for.

I'm a big fan of the Mi Band series of trackers, and this is the first device that finally got me to switch to something else. If you aren't familiar, Xiaomi and Huami aren't big brands in the US compared to other countries, but these are solid high quality products and not your standard fare Chinese junk. I've tried a LOT of different fitness trackers and smart watches- Everything from Google WearOS, Fitbit, Apple, and all the way down to the cheap trackers from Chinese throwaway brands with obscure apps. For a long time I've said I liked the features and quality of the expensive brands, but found they all had major flaws (battery life being a major one- I don't want another thing to charge as often as a phone!). The Mi band from Xiaomi was super affordable and high quality compared to others in that price range, and had a battery that only required being charged once a month.
This is basically the smarter older brother of that band. It is compatible with Mi Fit, so all my data transferred right over, but it is so much nicer than the band. For starters, the notification system is easier to read and keep up with messages, but the benefits go far beyond a larger screen. The music control is a nice touch, I like being able to pause and adjust the volume without taking my phone out of my pocket if playing on a BT speaker while I'm doing dishes, for example. The tracking is pretty accurate compared to other expensive brands, and while it doesn't support apps like Wear OS and Apple Watches, it has all the fitness functions you'd need built in already, including some fun widgets beyond the expected ones like a stopwatch, phone finder and even a compass! And unlike cheap brands, the UI is responsive and smooth. Not the smoothest out there for sure, but more than acceptably smooth considering how much a flagship smartwatch costs compared to this.
It has support for voice commands, but I honestly found that feature kind of gimmicky more than useful. The higher end version of this includes a speaker which might make the command function more useful as sort of a digital assistant, not to mention the ability to take phone calls from your wrist. But the model I got to try out lacks the speaker, which is a fine compromise for a cheaper price tag all things considered. The battery life at first was just OK, a few days on a charge if using lift-to-wake functions, but just as on my Mi Band tracker of old, I found if I turn off auto-wake and rely on using the button to wake the display, the battery life goes from counting in days to counting in weeks. That's the killer feature of this device- the ability to leave it on to track fitness and sleep habits without having to charge it so often. I'll have to charge it more than my old Mi Band's monthly top up for sure, probably at least 2x a month, but that's still very manageable.
So that's it, after years of loving my Mi Bands and considering it the standard by which all practical fitness trackers should be judged, I'm finally moving on to an Amazfit watch. This is a difficult value to beat.

I ended up having to supplement my own using 2 metal washers in the middle of the array of spacers. They could have avoided this by just including a couple more of their thin spacers to make up for the extra length for people like me, but at least I got it working. I like that the TV easily comes off using the pull tabs, and I'm thankful that my 48" TV is large enough to hide the pull strings. After installing the unit and using it for a few days it now has pop up ads on screen and wants you to purchase subscription services for extra features that were not mentioned in the description of the item. The ads make the unit difficult and unsafe to use while driving. We would not recommend this product.

ORGINAL INSTALL REVIEW BEFORE THE POP-UP ADS.
Pros: As the headline says, everything you need to install is included in the box including a backup camera and GPS antenna. The wire harness adapter is pre-wired to plug the unit directly into your factory harness/plugs without splicing any wires. It mounts directly up to the stock radio location without the use of any installation adapters or cutting plastics. The stock plastic trim plate aligns perfectly over the unit once installed and keeps a clean factory look. Optional RCA plug wire harnesses and USB tether plugs are also included for compatibility with your own custom aftermarket external sound equipment if needed. It works with both Apple CarPlay and Android Auto enabled cell phones. It can be used as a mobile Wi-Fi internet hotspot for passengers when paired with your cellphone. System updates can be downloaded directly to the unit through home or cell Wi-Fi once installed. If you have steering wheel controls, they can be manually programed from a menu on the unit to do the functions intended.

Cons: Menus are a little confusing and hard to find "while doing the initial radio setup". The EQ setting screen is hard to find and the HiFi setting (which acts a volume/bass boost) should be turned off if are using stock factory Jeep speakers. HiFi is turned on by default and it makes the volume level far too loud on the stock speakers at its lowest possible volume knob setting. Once the EQ and HiFi 0n/0ff settings are set to your ideal preferences you won’t need to navigate to the EQ screen again. Last minor con is when/how you exit your installed Aps. You’ll need to swipe them completely off the screen to stop them from running in the background and slowing the unit down similar to a cellphone.

Overall: Lots of features. Easy downloadable state maps for NAVI. Easy to download updates. Sounds better than the stock Jeep CD player once the EQ setting have been adjusted. Has a microphone intergraded into the faceplate. Easy to customize the display brightness, colors, wallpaper, and sounds. All the buttons/knobs are backlit with your headlight activation. It will play movies and MP3s.
